topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Alignment constrains where an object may begin, while padding helps satisfy those constraints within compound objects and arrays. These properties affect correctness before they affect speed. This chapter uses alignof and alignas to inspect and request alignment, then explains why a chosen sixty-four-byte boundary is an experimental layout choice rather than proof of the target processor’s cache-line size.

Padding might help, but it might also expand the working set enough to hurt a different workload.

topics.title: 6.1.1 Using alignof
topics.summary: alignof(T) reports the alignment requirement of T in bytes. An object must be placed at an address suitable for its type under the applicable allocation and lifetime rules. A raw byte buffer is not automatically suitable for every over-aligned object merely because it contains enough bytes.

topics.title: 6.1.2 Using alignas
topics.summary: alignas requests an alignment for an object or type, subject to language and implementation constraints. It can strengthen an alignment requirement but cannot validly weaken a type’s natural requirement. An aligned type’s size also accommodates array-element alignment, so requesting a large alignment can substantially increase the footprint of small objects.

blocks.text: alignas expresses an alignment requirement on a declaration where the language permits it. It can request stricter alignment; it is not a way to weaken a type’s natural requirement so an unsuitable address becomes valid. Unsupported or inconsistent requests are not portable optimization recipes. Keep alignment choices in a small representation layer and let compilation check whether the target accepts them.

blocks.text: Remember that increasing alignment can increase complete-object size. A private implementation detail can be revised with ordinary rebuilds; a separately distributed binary interface needs compatibility planning. Keep performance experiments private until their consequences are understood. The later professional volume develops ABI management; this chapter establishes why an apparently local alignas edit can have wider effects.

topics.title: 6.2.1 Understanding Cache-Line Boundaries
topics.summary: Processors transfer and coordinate cache data in implementation-specific units commonly called cache lines. Independent threads writing separate objects that share one coherence line can interfere through false sharing even when no C++ data race exists. Separating hot write locations can reduce that interaction for an appropriate workload.

blocks.text: Caches move and coordinate data in units that need not match C++ objects. When independent threads repeatedly modify distinct objects that fall in the same coherence unit, their updates can generate traffic even though the language considers the objects separate. This phenomenon is commonly called false sharing. It is a performance interaction, not automatically a C++ data race.

blocks.text: True contention is different: several threads intentionally access the same logical object or lock. Padding neighboring counters does not remove that shared dependency. Before changing layout, identify which object each thread reads and writes. A single global counter remains a shared update point even when it occupies a padded structure by itself.

blocks.text: Performance also depends on placement, scheduling, compiler optimization, update frequency, and surrounding work. A loop that repeatedly writes a private ordinary counter may be optimized into fewer stores, changing what the benchmark measures. A diagnostic design must ensure that the measured operation actually exists without introducing an unrelated synchronization bottleneck. Atomic per-thread counters can make updates observable for a specific experiment, but they also change the workload and must be described honestly.

A separate benchmark can compare compact and separated layouts under a stated workload. The acceptance test should verify final counts and report timing; it should not fail merely because one layout is not faster on a particular shared machine. Correctness is a stable contract here, while speed is an empirical result to interpret.

topics.title: 6.2.2 Avoiding Wasteful Padding
topics.summary: Padding can improve separation or satisfy alignment, but it also expands working sets. Reordering fields by alignment requirements may reduce internal gaps on a particular ABI. Separating hot and cold fields can reduce bytes touched during a critical loop, while padding every object can make a read-heavy workload slower by increasing cache pressure.

blocks.text: Choose layout based on access patterns and compatibility requirements. A public struct’s layout is an interface concern, so a private performance experiment should not silently become an ABI change. Record both sizeof and the measured workload result. Smaller and faster are related only under a particular operation and environment, not by definition.

blocks.text: Padding solves some placement problems by spending storage. It can also waste bandwidth and cache capacity when the program scans fields that do not need separation. A design with one padded object per reading might reduce interference during updates but force a reporting pass to touch many more cache lines. The correct choice depends on the dominant operations and their frequency.
rich: Padding solves some placement problems by spending storage. It can also waste bandwidth and cache capacity when the program scans fields that do not need separation. A design with one padded object per reading might reduce interference during updates but force a reporting pass to touch many more cache lines. The correct choice depends on the dominant operations and their frequency.

blocks.text: Field grouping offers another approach. Separate frequently updated counters from infrequently read metadata, or use a structure of arrays when operations process one field across many records. reading.title: 6.2.2 Avoiding Wasteful Padding
paragraphs: Padding can improve separation or satisfy alignment, but it also expands working sets. Reordering fields by alignment requirements may reduce internal gaps on a particular ABI. Separating hot and cold fields can reduce bytes touched during a critical loop, while padding every object can make a read-heavy workload slower by increasing cache pressure.

Choose layout based on access patterns and compatibility requirements. A public struct’s layout is an interface concern, so a private performance experiment should not silently become an ABI change. Record both sizeof and the measured workload result. Smaller and faster are related only under a particular operation and environment, not by definition.

Padding solves some placement problems by spending storage. It can also waste bandwidth and cache capacity when the program scans fields that do not need separation. A design with one padded object per reading might reduce interference during updates but force a reporting pass to touch many more cache lines. The correct choice depends on the dominant operations and their frequency.

Field grouping offers another approach. Separate frequently updated counters from infrequently read metadata, or use a structure of arrays when operations process one field across many records.
